summary: Describes the Network Trouble Ticket Data Model, a way to exchange trouble tickets between organizations with different procedures and systems, motivated by multi-domain grid projects. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: When several companies run parts of one network, each has its own way of writing up problems. This gives them a common form.

subtitle: A normalized data format for exchanging network trouble tickets across administrative domains.

tldr.problem: Multi-domain networks and grids involve many operators with different trouble ticket systems, formats, and procedures. Normalizing tickets at a central NOC is difficult without a common format.
tldr.mechanism: NTTDM defines a standardized XML representation for trouble tickets with fixed fields for origin, severity, status, impact, and timeline information, allowing different NOCs to exchange tickets and automate processing.
tldr.outcome: Originally designed for the EGEE grid project, NTTDM provides a flexible experimental model that balances required standardization with adaptation to different domains' needs.

today: RFC 6137 remains an experimental specification designed for grid and multi-domain network operations. It was developed and validated within the EGEE project and is available for adoption by other similar multi-domain projects.

sections.title: The Trouble Ticket Challenge
sections.content:
The EGEE (Enabling Grids for E-sciencE) project operated as a multi-domain grid spanning European National Research and Educational Networks (NRENs). Each partner network had its own trouble ticket system, procedures, and terminology. The central EGEE Network Operation Centre (ENOC) received hundreds of tickets monthly from different sources but had no common way to process, filter, store, or analyze them.

The challenge: each NOC thought about trouble in its own way—what one organization calls 'link failure', another might describe as 'access line fault'. Automation was nearly impossible without a common format and terminology.

The NTTDM solves this by defining a standardized data model with a single XML Schema. Each domain still uses its own local trouble ticket system, but when tickets enter the central NOC, they are normalized into NTTDM format. This enables the central NOC to filter, sort, store, and analyze all tickets uniformly.
sections.plainLanguage: Different networks describe problems differently. NTTDM gives them a standard form where everyone fills in the same boxes—problem type, priority, when it started, who found it—so the central office can sort and organize them all together.

sections.title: The Data Model Structure
sections.content:
NTTDM is specified as both an abstract data model (described in UML) and an XML Schema implementation. The model contains two main classes:

NTTDM-Document: The root container representing a single XML document. It carries a version (always '1.00') and language information, and contains one or more Ticket elements.

Ticket: Represents a single trouble incident. A ticket has 29 defined fields organized into logical groups: origin information (which domain sent it, original ID), basic information (title, type, priority, status), timing information (when opened, closed, detected, reported), impact assessment, related issues, location/network details, contact engineers, and a cryptographic hash for integrity.

Each field is characterized by four attributes: a description, a TYPE (Defined, Free, Multiple, or List), a VALID FORMAT (Predefined String, String, or Datetime), and whether it is MANDATORY.
sections.plainLanguage: Every trouble ticket is an XML document with a structured format. It has fields for who reported the problem, what the problem is, how serious it is, what affected parts of the network, who is working on it, and when various things happened.

sections.title: Key Fields and Semantics
sections.content:
Ticket origin: PARTNER_ID identifies the sending organization (one of the partner NOCs), and ORIGINAL_ID is the ticket's ID in the home system. Together they form the unique NTTDM TT_ID as PARTNER_ID_ORIGINAL_ID.

Ticket type and priority: TT_TYPE categorizes tickets as Operational (network incidents), Informational (maintenance/upgrade notices), Administrative (access/credential issues), or Test. TT_PRIORITY is Low, Medium, or High.

Problem description: TT_SHORT_DESCRIPTION uses predefined values like 'Core Line Fault', 'Access Line Fault', 'Router Hardware Fault', 'Network Congestion', etc. TT_LONG_DESCRIPTION is free text for details.

Status and transitions: TT_STATUS tracks the ticket lifecycle with nine states (Opened, Updated, Closed, Solved, Inactive, Cancelled, Reopened, Superseded, Opened/Closed). The model defines legal state transitions and identifies terminal states marked with (X).

Timing: Multiple datetime fields track the incident timeline: TT_OPEN_DATETIME, START_DATETIME (when incident began), DETECT_DATETIME, REPORT_DATETIME, END_DATETIME, and TT_CLOSE_DATETIME. Optional WORK_PLAN fields document planned resolution windows.

Impact assessment: A predefined field with values ranging from 'No impact' through 'Reduced redundancy', 'Performance impact' (minor or severe), 'No connectivity', 'On backup', 'At risk', and 'Unknown'.

Network details: Optional fields identify the AFFECTED_COMMUNITY (set of users), AFFECTED_SERVICE, LOCATION, NETWORK_NODE, and NETWORK_LINK_CIRCUIT involved.
sections.plainLanguage: A ticket records who had the problem, what kind of problem it was, how serious it was, when things happened, what parts of the network it affected, and what the impact was. Each field has a fixed set of allowed values or free text as appropriate.

sections.title: Automation and Workflow
sections.content:
One major benefit of NTTDM is enabling automation. A typical workflow:

1. Different NOCs send tickets in their native formats to the central NOC. 2. A normalization process converts them to NTTDM XML. 3. The central NOC filters, sorts, and stores normalized tickets in a database. 4. The system assesses the ticket's impact on the grid. 5. Tickets are pushed to dashboards, analysis tools, and the EGEE ticket system.

Because all tickets are now in the same format, the central NOC can automatically determine which tickets are related (using RELATED_ACTIVITY and RELATED_EXTERNAL_TICKETS), track patterns across domains, and detect when multiple tickets describe the same underlying problem in the grid.

The HISTORY field allows adding timestamped comments about actions taken, supporting collaborative troubleshooting across domains.
sections.plainLanguage: When the central office receives a problem ticket, it translates it to NTTDM format, then can automatically organize it, figure out what it impacts, connect it to related problems, and track how it's being fixed.

sections.title: Design Philosophy and Status
sections.content:
NTTDM was designed with three principles: being effective and comprehensive to serve multiple NOC styles, flexible to allow domain-specific extensions while maintaining core standardization, and pragmatic about free-form content (human description fields) vs. automated processing (predefined types and dates).

The model does not try to capture every possible field each domain might use. Instead, it provides ADDITIONAL_DATA and RELATED_ACTIVITY fields to link tickets to domain-specific external information. This allows each domain to keep its detailed local records while the central NOC maintains a uniform view.

RFC 6137 is published as experimental. The authors note that the model was successfully used within EGEE, and other grids are invited to use it and report feedback. The plan was to gain operational experience before potentially advancing it to the Standards Track.
sections.plainLanguage: NTTDM was designed to be good enough for real use but open enough that different grids and networks can adapt it to their needs. It's marked experimental so people can try it out and suggest improvements.
